A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dataset and iterative shadow–light framework, with matching core equations and experimental tables despite the changed title and format. All pages are readable. V2 includes supplementary material absent from the supplied v1 PDF.

before.justification: V1 reports original shadow-detection comparisons, qualitative predictions, and geometry, iteration, and loss ablations in Section 5.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original cross-dataset predictions, light-estimation evaluations, and a shadow-removal user study.

M1.justification: The detection architecture, iterative feedback, and training losses remain unchanged. Section 5.4 adds a downstream procedure using ShadowFormer with joint-mask removal followed by attached-mask refinement within the object region. Supplementary architecture descriptions document the existing detector rather than establish a redesign.

E1.justification: V2 extends evaluation beyond the curated detection dataset to SRD images, SBU-TimeLapse static-scene videos, and ViSha dynamic-scene videos. It also evaluates downstream shadow removal through human preferences. These introduce substantial coverage of new data environments and task requirements; the original training sources remain.

E2.justification: The seven detection methods and four fine-tuned baselines in main Table 2 are retained. Supplementary Table 1 adds BDRAR†+Normal and SILT†+Normal. New experiments also compare against a standalone light estimator supplied with ground-truth masks and joint-mask ShadowFormer removal. These supplement the existing comparison suite.

E3.justification: New protocols include independent framewise video inference, light-direction MAE evaluation on 42 calibrated WSRD test images, and a randomized preference study with a 40-question pool, 20 questions per participant, and 259 collected votes. V2 also reports shadow/non-shadow error breakdowns. The original training budget and split remain unchanged. CUHK's reported contribution changes from 538 to 528 images, reconciling the stated total without establishing that images were removed.

E4.justification: V2 adds evidence testing whether normal inputs help competing detectors, whether iterative feedback improves light estimation relative to a ground-truth-mask control, and whether predictions generalize to changing shadows in videos. The original geometry, iteration, and loss ablations remain. The earlier multi-object pairing failure example is omitted.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's vote totals and preference percentages are new results, while question randomization is an evaluation-design addition; neither introduces uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Main Tables 2–3 retain their numerical results. Newly reported outcomes include 80.7% preference for separate-mask refinement (209/259 votes), light MAE of 0.061, 0.050, and 0.049 across iterations versus 0.034 with ground-truth masks, normal-augmented baseline scores, additional runtime entries, and cross-dataset predictions. Some duplicated values disagree: BDRAR attached F1 is 53.32 in main Table 2 but 52.32 in supplementary Table 1, leaving the intended value unresolved.

T1.justification: The single-directional-light assumption, normal–light dot-product rule, and loss mathematics are retained. V2 combines the three light-loss equations into one numbered equation. Additional geometry-preparation details document existing operations rather than introduce substantive theory, proofs, or derivations.

C1.justification: The joint framework, iterative refinement, annotated dataset, and at-least-33% attached-BER reduction claims remain. V2's introduction adds a concrete claim that separate masks improve shadow removal. Its conclusion more specifically emphasizes improved attached detection while maintaining strong cast performance.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of video examples as temporal robustness and the ground-truth-mask light estimator as an approximate performance bound. It expands lighting limitations to extended sources and strong indirect illumination, but removes the explicit limitation about associating cast and attached shadows with individual objects. The central geometry-based explanation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: The new supplement documents the PVT-b5 encoder, input/output adaptations, SBU initialization, 0.05 encoder learning-rate multiplier, TITAN RTX hardware and two-GPU training, normal computation, annotation corrections, and light-direction construction. V2 also adds a project-page address. These substantially expand reproducibility information without demonstrating changes to the underlying implementation.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion of MetaShadow and directional-light video research, plus references supporting ShadowFormer, depth estimation, and the encoder. Several classical shadow/illumination references are removed. The main positioning against methods that merge or overlook attached shadows remains intact.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten, with stronger application-led motivation. Problem setup and framework descriptions are consolidated, method subsections are reorganized, and dedicated generalization, application, and supplementary sections reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout and substantially rearranges existing figures. V1's problem-setup example reappears in supplementary Figure 12. V2 adds removal, video, light-estimation, and dataset-curation displays, groups the ablation table by topic, and introduces expanded supplementary tables.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1 by quantitatively evaluating the claimed light-estimation feedback, adding geometry-informed comparison controls, and supplying substantial architecture and dataset-curation details. Cross-dataset examples and the removal study broaden supporting evidence without changing the original benchmark scores. These gains outweigh the dropped instance-pairing caveat and reporting weaknesses, including inconsistent duplicated scores, unclear normal/light coordinate conventions, and incomplete user-study uncertainty reporting.
